The field of machine learning (ML) is rapidly expanding, with new applications and ethical concerns emerging in parallel. This paper examines three key metrics—fairness, federated learning, and privacy (differential privacy)—that offer solutions to critical ethical issues within ML applications. Specifically, federated learning enhances fairness by mitigating algorithmic bias against minority groups, while differential privacy safeguards individual privacy by preventing the identification of individuals from sensitive data. We evaluate these approaches by analyzing their synergies and limitations, aiming to provide a comprehensive overview of how these concepts address ethical challenges in ML.

We investigate a model featuring a $U(1)_X$ gauge symmetry that couples to the Standard Model via the $Z'$ boson and to a real scalar field, which acquires a mass through a spontaneous $U(1)_X$ symmetry breaking. In this framework, dark matter consists of the lightest $Z'$-charged fermion, while the scalar's remnants appear as light pseudoscalar states within the spectrum. We analyze how the $Z'$ resonance impacts both direct detection and collider searches for dark matter, while also examining the relationship between the dark matter and the light pseudoscalars. We demonstrate that the presence of $Z'$ resonances can alleviate constraints from dark matter direct detection searches, and that the presence of light pseudoscalars can suppress the dark matter relic density, thereby satisfying Planck limits. Additionally, we explore the phenomenology of the $Z'$ resonance near scalar-pseudoscalar production thresholds, which can lead to an apparent lightness of the $Z'$ in collider experiments.

Deep unsupervised learning (DUL) has recently emerged as a powerful tool capable of uncovering intricate relationships within data, offering a viable alternative to traditional genetic algorithms (GA) in diverse wireless communication scenarios. This paper examines the efficacy of DUL in unsupervised learning channel state information (CSI) recovery for millimeter-wave massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems. We demonstrate that DUL can effectively extract data patterns and outperform standard GA approaches. Furthermore, we illustrate that DUL not only yields superior performance but also delivers a significant reduction in both computational complexity and implementation cost.

The study investigates the $\beta^-$ decay of $^{132}$Sn, utilizing recent experimental data on the post-decay gamma rays from the excited states of $^{132}$Xe. By applying a newly developed statistical model, researchers have derived the $\beta^-$-decay matrix elements for the transitions to the ground state and the first 10 excited states of $^{132}$Xe. The analysis demonstrates that beta strength is governed by the combined configurations of the parent and daughter nuclei. Additionally, matrix elements for the excited states align well with prior findings from shell model calculations. These results offer valuable insights into the beta-decay process in $^{132}$Sn, a nucleus of critical importance in nuclear astrophysics.

We investigate a straightforward extension to the Standard Model that incorporates a complex singlet scalar field alongside three right-handed neutrinos. Within this framework, the scalar field accounts for dark matter, while the right-handed neutrinos are proposed as origin for active left-handed neutrinos. Although the relic density requirement for dark matter does not necessitate a large mixing angle between the singlet scalar and the Higgs boson, a non-zero mixing angle is required to establish a viable mechanism for generating right-handed neutrinos. We analyze the implications of this scenario within the context of the lepton flavor violation process $ \mu \to e \gamma $. We find that $ \mu \to e \gamma $ can be generated through an effective dimension-6 Weinberg operator, which is mediated by loops involving both the singlet scalar and the right-handed neutrinos. We determine that the flavor violation can be adequately explained if the right-handed neutrino mass spectrum lies in the keV to MeV range.

This research investigates control algorithms rooted in machine learning, specifically examining their capacity for generalization and their reliance on data efficiency. The study evaluates three approaches: a model-free reinforcement learning (RL) method, a model-based RL technique, and a model-based controller utilizing Gaussian processes. These algorithms are applied to control a nonlinear pendulum system subjected to unmodeled disturbances and system uncertainties. The experiments demonstrate that the model-based control strategies surpass their model-free RL counterparts in terms of generalization. Furthermore, it is established that even when limited by the amount of available training data, these model-based algorithms generate superior performance relative to traditional model-free RL methods.

We establish the spin-three Ward identities within the framework of Ward's theorem for Toda conformal field theories, which explicitly define the higher-spin symmetry algebra. These identities serve to relate higher-spin correlation functions and may help derive their recursive structure. Our demonstration further supports the consistency of the proposed closed form of the Toda conformal field.

We introduce a GAN model incorporating a relation network (RN) that leverages pairwise image features to synthesize diverse views of objects within a single scene. By utilizing an RN-based relational discriminator, our model learns coherent image features representing shared properties across different angles, enabling the generation of varied perspectives for the same object or scene. The RN architecture also facilitates one-to-many image mapping, which enhances state-of-the-art image diversity within generated classes. Empirical results from our model, trained on ShapeNet and the COCO datasets for 3D shape and 2D image segmentation respectively, demonstrate superior State-of-the-Art performance in image generation diversity compared to existing methods.

We introduce an enhanced twin-field quantum key distribution method that utilizes reference frames to mitigate the impact of phase noise. This strategy not only facilitates the creation of a global phase reference but also enables the efficient, linear scalability of coherent states. By jointly leveraging individual phase references and local phase noise references, our approach achieves a secure key rate proportional to the loss in single spans, outperforming previous protocols limited to pulse-level interference.
This work examines the symbol spaces for Toeplitz operators acting on $p$-Bergman and $p$-Fock spaces.

In object detection, the quality of bounding-box annotations is crucial for model performance. However, in scenarios involving scarce or costly labels, such as in medical imaging, obtaining high-quality data is often impractical. This study investigates the use of pseudo-bounding-boxes generated by state-of-the-art segmentation models to enhance detectors. Our experiments on the breast imaging dataset, MIMIC-CXR, demonstrate that training detectors using these segmented regions significantly improves detection performance. Furthermore, we evaluate the impact of modifying standard loss functions to better align with the characteristics of these pseudo-bounding-boxes.

Self-absorption significantly impacts the spectral observations of ionized and neutral gas within star-influenced regions, often obscuring the physical characteristics of those environments. This study utilizes the 3D hydrodynamics code RAMSES to model the interaction between a massive star and a giant molecular cloud (GMC), specifically examining the effects of self-absorption on the resulting spectra. We generated synthetic spectra for the 21 cm hyperfine line of neutral hydrogen (HI) and the [O I] 63 $\mu$m fine-structure line of ionized oxygen, incorporating cloud properties and stellar parameters. By comparing these synthetic spectra with models that neglect self-absorption, we quantified the distortion's magnitude. Results indicate that the observed spectral profiles are substantially altered by self-absorption, frequently producing double-peaked structures. Furthermore, the intensity of these synthetic spectra varies with distance from the cloud's center, demonstrating that the distortion's severity is a function of the specific cloud parameters examined.

Transformer models have largely superseded convolutional networks in many computer vision applications due to their flexibility in learning representations. However, this adaptability stems from their minimal inductive biases compared to the latter. To address this limitation, we introduce a theory of attention-based inductive biases, demonstrating that these biases can be implemented as specialized attention mechanisms. Furthermore, we show that these learned biases facilitate more efficient training and improved performance. Empirically, we introduce a specific bias derived from the concept of "receptive paths"—an attention mechanism that biases the learning of specific receptive path structures. Our experiments reveal that these path-biased Transformers successfully acquire the expected path architectures, offering a clear illustration of how inductive biases function.

Although classical mortality models typically incorporate time-varying factor loadings, recent predictive distributions derived directly from these extensions often fail to account for the uncertainty associated with the estimated parameters. This study proposes a new approach to jointly sample both the latent factor levels and their time-varying loadings within a Bayesian framework. The proposed method is evaluated using synthetic data and data from England and Wales, as well as data from the German states. The results demonstrate that predictive performance surpasses that of standard models and highlight a significant discrepancy between point forecasts and the broader range of possible distributional outcomes.

This study introduces a novel approach to neural architecture search (NAS) specifically designed to handle interference within pre-trained language models. By employing a two-stage optimization framework, we first conduct a two-way NAS to identify the optimal inter- and intra-layer architectures for a target task. Subsequently, a NAS-focused learning strategy is applied to jointly fine-tune the inter- and intra-layer structures. Our experiments, which test the proposed method on RoBERTa and ELECTRA baselines, reveal that our technique surpasses existing solutions by 1.5% and 2.2% relative performance gains, respectively. Additionally, we executed a computational efficiency analysis, demonstrating that our method reduces the total training cost by 20% compared to current state-of-the-art baselines.

Time-series feature extraction tools are essential for extracting time-domain characteristics from data, yet the current state-of-the-art package, TSFEED, faces limitations. TSFEED struggles with processing heterogeneous data formats and executing custom extractors, and it relies on the computationally expensive Dynamic Time Warping for distance measurement. We introduce "theft," an open-source Python library that not only supports various input formats and custom extraction logic but also accelerates computation by parallelizing the process. Additionally, theft integrates established time-series anomalies detection methods. Benchmark tests indicate that theft is significantly faster than TSFEED while producing comparable results. The library is freely available for use and can be found at the GitHub repository linked in the original text.

We establish that for proper geodesic complete CAT(0) spaces, geodesic completeness can be characterized as a property of the associated fundamental group. Building on this, we derive an existence theorem demonstrating that every finitely generated group can be represented as the fundamental group of a proper, geodesic complete CAT(0) space. Furthermore, we prove a non-existence result: if a group $\Gamma$ acts geometrically on a proper CAT(0) space $X$ with an abelian or surface group $\Gamma_1$ as a proper subgroup, then the action cannot leave $\Gamma_1$ quasi-convex within $X$.

Translation quality assessment (TQA) is a critical component of the localization workflow, serving to evaluate the competence of translators and auditors. Traditionally, a human assessor evaluates a translated document to determine its quality, a process that is labor-intensive and costly. To address these limitations, automated TQA methods have emerged, which typically rely on machine learning algorithms to predict quality scores based on linguistic features. This study introduces a data-driven approach to automatically evaluating machine translation that incorporates a feature-based scoring mechanism. Specifically, the feature matrix includes source and target sentence embeddings, alignment information, and candidate translations. The proposed system was tested on the English-German subset of the TED Talk dataset, yielding an accuracy of 0.86, a recall of 0.84, and an F1-score of 0.85.

This study examines how light scatters when multiple modes interact randomly with a compact object composed of numerous independent scatterers. We demonstrate that the characteristic eigenchannels correspond directly to specific intensity distributions inside both the object and the far field. These findings offer new insights into how light propagates through opaque materials and provide practical guidelines for controlling light transmission in various media.

Neural networks are increasingly vital for visual tasks, yet their inference latency remains a significant hurdle. While prior research has primarily focused on pruning the first and last convolutional layers to accelerate inference, this work introduces an approach that leverages iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) to remove kernels from intermediate layers as well. We demonstrate that applying IMP across all depths substantially decreases computational load without compromising accuracy. Furthermore, this method is versatile, successfully adapting to various network architectures, including ResNet, Inception, InResNet, InNet, and VGG.

Although the odds of winning in the UK National Lottery are approximately 1 in 139 million, the potential jackpots can reach amounts exceeding £100 million. By analyzing the trade-off between these prizes and the probability of victory, we demonstrate that there is a specific positive return threshold within the £30 to £50 million jackpot range. This finding suggests that, contrary to the prevailing belief that purchasing tickets is always financially unwise, buying tickets can be a rational economic decision when such mid-range jackpots are awarded.

We conduct a comprehensive large-charge expansion for the $O(2)\times O(2)$ model, deriving the equation of state and critical exponents. These findings are compared against results derived from Monte-Carlo simulations and $\epsilon$-expansions. Additionally, we apply a large-charge expansion to the 3D Heisenberg model, examining critical exponents and the amplitude ratio of the susceptibility. All derived results are benchmarked against Monte-Carlo simulation data.

Valley Hall transport in monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides is typically attributed to nonuniform strain. However, this study reveals that a finite, non-uniform magnetic field also influences this transport. Specifically, the effect of non-magnetic field strain is significantly enhanced when the valley Hall conductance is small, meaning the magnetic contribution becomes a crucial factor in such cases. Furthermore, the article proposes a new experimental method to distinguish between these two causes.

Model soups have become a widely adopted technique for aggregating multiple trained models to enhance performance. While recent research primarily investigates optimal aggregation strategies to maximize accuracy, there remains limited understanding of how these methods handle the trade-off between overfitting and out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization. In this work, we explore this gap by examining the impact of various aggregation techniques on the distributional shift resilience of adaptive domain models. Our findings indicate that simple averaging is suboptimal, whereas advanced aggregation schemes can yield further improvements in generalization. Additionally, we propose a novel approach called "MLP-Soup," which utilizes a multi-layer perceptron to aggregate model outputs, demonstrating that it surpasses conventional aggregation methods. To support these findings, we introduce a comprehensive benchmark suite featuring ten state-of-the-art domain adaptation methods evaluated across six datasets.

t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE) is a prevalent algorithm for visualizing high-dimensional spherical data by mapping local Gaussian distributions to local Gaussian distributions. However, many spherical datasets exhibit local structures that deviate from Gaussian characteristics. To address this, we propose a model that substitutes the Gaussian distribution with a generalized elliptical distribution for local proximity in spherical data. We developed a modified t-SNE that leverages these generalized elliptical distributions for local density estimation, demonstrating through experiments that this approach yields more accurate representations of the data's local structure.

This study examines the polaron $Z$ factor within the one-component liquid helium model, employing a diagrammatic approach that extends beyond simple contact interactions to include dipole-dipole forces. Our results indicate that the polaron $Z$ factor derived from the complete diagrammatic series deviates significantly from the diagrammatic two-particle excitation (one-particle-hole) term across weak, intermediate, and strong coupling regimes. Specifically, while strong coupling interactions yield a deviation of 20% to 30% across all values, strong coupling forces produce a minimal discrepancy of just 5%. These findings imply that including only the one-particle-hole term is insufficient for accurately capturing the polaron behavior under strong coupling conditions involving dipole-dipole forces.

The digital-analog quantum computing strategy enables the emulation of numerous physical systems by executing specific interactions digitally while implementing others analogically. This research utilizes that approach to simulate the Fermi-Hubbard model, a quantity of significant interest for understanding high-temperature superconductivity. We propose a quantum circuit architecture that establishes the required digital-analog evolution through a sequence of digital gates interleaved with the digital coupling of Rb$^{138}$ atoms and cavity modes within a digital quantum-Lundee setup. By employing this method, we achieve the simulation of the Fermi-Hubbard model in a two-mode cavity, addressing the approach's initial prototype stage. Furthermore, we examine how variations in the parameters of the digital gates influence the system's dynamics.
We present a characterization theorem for matching polynomials that applies to both complete graphs and complete bipartite graphs.

This study examines the connections between mapping class group elements' quantum representations and their pseudo-Anosov counterparts. Specifically, we demonstrate that for any fixed simple closed curve, the magnitude of its quantum representation corresponding to a pseudo-Anosov element grows unboundedly as the curve length on a surface increases. Additionally, we establish that curve link eigenvalues within the mapping class group representation tend toward generic values when the curve link lengthens.

The transition to Scrum and other agile frameworks has become a primary strategy for organizations to boost efficiency and project success. However, the onset of the global pandemic forced a swift adoption of remote working, introducing significant new obstacles to this already complex adoption process. This study examines how a software firm in Brazil managed Scrum implementation during the initial phase of forced remote employment caused by the pandemic. Utilizing a case study design, the research employed interviews and document analysis to identify and address the specific challenges encountered. The findings indicate that the success of Scrum implementation is heavily contingent upon effective project management, particularly the management of communication and the mitigation of scope creep. Ultimately, the case study highlights the critical necessity of tailored training and coaching to manage these complexities, particularly within the context of remote teams.

The article presents a formula for the Guess-Wu number of arrowhead matrices over any field in characteristic zero, derived through a combinatorial approach. This solution connects strictly with the Gau–Wu number by demonstrating it aligns perfectly through a rigorous comparison.

The mass difference between the $B_d^0$ and $B_s^0$ mesons, $\Delta m_{B_s-B_p}$, is a key observable in $B$-meson physics. This measurement relies on determining the time difference ($\Delta t_{B_s-B_p}$) between two $B$-decays, which requires an accurate measurement of each meson's proper decay time. This study introduces an enhanced method for measuring these decay times and demonstrates that it is applicable to both $B_s$ and $B_d$ mesons. The method's validity is confirmed using data from $B_s$ and $B_d$ candidates, as well as from other background events. By comparing the reconstructed proper decay lengths, we show that the $B_s$ and $B_d$ mesons exhibit similar distributions, distinct from those of other sources. The results indicate that the proposed technique achieves a precision of 1.5% for $B_s$ and 1.6% for $B_d$, matching the accuracy of current methods.

This study introduces a novel approach to analyzing color-based interactions within persistent homology by adapting the colored single-linkage clustering algorithm proposed by Cohen-Steiner et al. to simplicial complexes. We extend this adaptation to create a colored Rips complex, which serves as the foundation for a colored persistent homology analysis. By adapting the concept of persistence into this colored framework, we define persistence intervals for individual colored simplices. We then construct a persistence matrix that tracks the lifespan of these colored simplices throughout the filtration process. Finally, we apply persistent color barcodes to represent the stability of color classes over time.

This study investigates the computational complexity inherent in power control for binary networks. We introduce a gap analysis between the optimal solution and the best-known approximation to evaluate performance degradation. Our analysis demonstrates that within large interference networks, binary power control achieves nearly the same performance as optimal power control. We also prove that the gap between any two networks sharing identical interference patterns is negligible. These theoretical findings are substantiated by simulation results.

Financial audits are a critical component of the accounting profession, yet the extensive volume of data and records often makes the auditing process difficult. While current audit software has largely automated routine tasks, it has not significantly addressed the challenges of human judgment and decision-making. This study introduces a new approach to financial auditing by integrating a data mining technique that incorporates uncertainty management. This method utilizes a specialized uncertainty model to capture the variability inherent in auditing decisions. By applying this framework, the researchers employ a Dempter-Shafer mass function to represent the differing interests and perspectives of various stakeholders involved in auditing. Additionally, the Demptran rule is applied to the method to ensure the consistency of the uncertainty model. The proposed technique is validated through a case study that demonstrates the application of the method to a specific auditing scenario.

We propose a novel efficient simulation technique for point processes termed "Acceptance Rejection Stitching." This method integrates multiple probability distribution functions (PDFs) to cover the full support of a target distribution, allowing for accurate point process generation. Each function represents a partial PDF valid over a specific domain. By combining these approaches, we create a robust framework applicable to diverse point process types. The method's theoretical validity is established, and its practical performance is validated through simulations of Poisson, Cox, and Matern cluster processes. Additionally, we demonstrate that ARS significantly surpasses standard simulation methods in computational speed.

The Generalized Uncertainty Principle (GUP) offers a quantum-gravitational framework that modifies the behavior of phase space, thereby inducing deformations in Galilean transformations. In this study, we extend these transformations into the relativistic domain by deriving GUP-modified Lorentz transformations and examining their properties. Our results indicate that the GUP-introduced deviations affect only the transverse components of momentum and the parallel component of energy, leaving the internal structure of particles invariant. Consequently, fundamental symmetries such as CPT and CP are preserved. Furthermore, we analyze the relativistic dispersion relation derived from these transformations and evaluate their phenomenological implications.

Scheduling algorithms are pivotal for efficiently allocating processing power across computing devices, a challenge that becomes more complex with multitasking environments where users can share processing capacity at a granular level. By allowing users to determine their own preferred degree of access—ranging from full exclusive control down to no direct user involvement—we investigate how varying ratios of shared processing capacity influence scheduling outcomes. Specifically, this study examines scheduling strategies for cloud-based virtual machines (VMs) that support such flexible user policies. We analyze the interplay between different schedulers and user-defined sharing preferences, evaluating how policy choices affect scheduling performance metrics. The research also explores the relationship between these policies and user satisfaction, ultimately providing a framework for selecting optimal configurations to achieve a balanced trade-off between overall system performance and user well-being.

This study introduces a feedback control strategy for legged robots traversing soft surfaces, derived from a finite element-based soft ground model. To ensure robust performance, the feedback loop addresses linearization errors and external disturbances by employing a disturbance observer. The primary control objective is precise trajectory tracking, which is facilitated by a computed torque method combined with a feedforward compensator. This compensator iteratively forecasts and mitigates disturbances arising from soft ground interactions. Simulation results indicate that this approach enables rapid and accurate recovery from perturbations, whereas the open-loop controller fails to track the desired path effectively.

Firmware updates are critical for the operational continuity of IoT systems, yet large-scale deployments often struggle with scalability and reliability challenges. Concurrent Transmissions (CT) offer a solution by enabling parallel file transfers, thereby reducing overall update duration. This study evaluates the CT protocol's scalability and reliability specifically for IoT update scenarios. It introduces a novel CT protocol designed for IoT updates, which was tested in controlled environments ranging from 50 to 500 nodes. Results indicate that CT can increase update capacity by a factor of 10 with only a 10% increase in packet loss compared to traditional sequential transmissions. Additionally, CT was found to improve reliability by 25% under high-loss conditions compared to sequential transmissions. These findings suggest that CT is a promising approach for scalable and reliable IoT updates.

We examine the spatial self-similarity of self-energy and energy eigenfunctions in many-body localized (MBL) systems, specifically investigating how the fractonic dimension linked to self-energy evolves across the thermal-MBL transition and its relationship to the ratio of fractal dimensions of eigenfunctions. Our findings indicate that this self-energy fractal dimension is strictly less than one in both thermal and MBL phases, dropping to approximately 0.65 near criticality and reaching roughly 1.25 deep within the MBL regime. Additionally, we observe that absolute values of this self-energy fractal dimension are lower than those derived from the absolute squared of eigenfunctions on the same scale. These results underscore the critical role of self-energy fractal dimension in characterizing the MBL phase and its proximity to the transition point.

We introduce an enhanced algorithm, kBM-DP+, which adapts the dynamic programming approach of the original kBM-DP for solving MultipleTargets. This method streamlines the process by merging and optimizing overlapping subproblems, yielding a significant reduction in both time and space complexity. We demonstrate that kBM-DP+ retains the same capability to locate an exact solution for the MultipleTargets problem. Additionally, the kBM-DP+ approach is applied to the MultiColorSubsets and MultiPartition problems, with experimental results indicating that it substantially outperforms the standard kBM-DP in terms of efficiency.

This study examines the vulnerability of quantum classifiers to adversarial examples. We find evidence that even minute, often imperceptible changes to input data can drastically alter quantum classifier predictions. Furthermore, our results indicate that training via circuit compression may offer a viable strategy for improving the robustness of these models.

This study investigates the Steklov eigenvalues of a 3-dimensional unit-sphere domain featuring a surface perturbation, $D_\varepsilon$. We demonstrate that the normalized $l$-th Steklov eigenvalue, defined as $\lambda_l(D_\varepsilon)/\pi^2$, converges to its counterpart, $\lambda_l(B^3)/\pi^2$, at a rate of $O(\varepsilon^2)$ provided $l$ is not a perfect square. Conversely, if $k$ is a perfect square and $l=4k$, the normalized eigenvalue exhibits an oscillation of magnitude $O(\varepsilon^{1/2})$. These findings are substantiated by the derivation of explicit formulas for the oscillatory terms, which rely on the Fourier coefficients of the perturbation.

We introduce a novel approach to aligning executions of processes defined by their control flow graphs, which generalizes existing techniques that rely on call graphs. While traditional methods align only on calls and returns, and current state-of-the-art approaches additionally consider variable states, our approach inquires about the relative temporal order of all edges within the control flow graph. Specifically, we define three distinct types of alignments based on the direction of these considered edges: infix, postfix, and prefix. In infix and prefix variants, we evaluate the order of all nodes and edges; in postfix alignment, we consider only the order of edges, disregarding node states. We developed a new alignment algorithm capable of handling infix and prefix models, which we validated through the analysis of malware behavior.

The rapid expansion of wireless communication systems has necessitated more accurate radio propagation models to enhance network planning and coverage. Traditional modeling techniques are often labor-intensive and prone to inaccuracies caused by the complex geometry of urban radio environments. This study introduces a deep convolutional neural network (CNN) designed to predict 5G radio propagation, demonstrating that it surpasses conventional modeling in both speed and precision. The research evaluates the model's efficacy using real-world datasets from diverse geographic areas and varying topographies. Results indicate that the deep CNN approach yields lower error rates than traditional methods, with mean percentage errors of 1.8% for received signal power and 1.4% for signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR). Furthermore, the model exhibits robustness against variations in the density of radio environment data.

While contemporary temporal planning systems have achieved significant success, they frequently overlook the validation of both their planners and solvers. This paper introduces a novel, efficient algorithm for validating temporal planning solutions. This method is employed by PyTP, an open-source framework available at https://github.com/sophiarastogi/PyTP, which supports the Python 3 language. This tool enables users to develop planners, solvers, and solve problems within Python 3. By utilizing PyTP's validation capabilities, developers can ensure the correctness of their algorithms and the accuracy of solutions, particularly for complex scenarios involving time.

This study introduces a two-stage adaptive robust optimization approach designed to allocate generation and storage capacities within transmission-constrained, time-resolved power systems. By assuming only statistical mean and variance for load and renewable generation, a tractable robust optimization problem is derived. A mean-variance decomposition technique is employed to generate an efficient solution for the resulting model. A two-stage adaptive framework further refines this solution, yielding a near-optimal result and revealing insights into temporal resolution impacts on capacity planning costs and capacity reallocation errors due to time discretization. Numerical experiments on IEEE 30- and 118-bus systems demonstrate that misallocation errors are highly sensitive to time resolution, with coarse granularity potentially causing significant over- and under-procurement of generation capacity.

This study establishes the global existence of weak solutions for the two-dimensional scalar Vlasov-Poisson system in both periodic domains and space-periodic with fixed charge distributions. The problem is formulated as an initial-boundary value problem defined on $\mathbb{R}^2 \times [0, \infty)$ with velocity space $\mathbb{v} \in \mathbb{R}^2$ and a suitable spatial domain, subject to specific moment conditions on the initial distribution of measures. The existence of these weak solutions for the measure-valued solution of scalar Vlasov-Poisson equations is derived by utilizing a compactness method based on an approximation scheme involving smooth solutions in Sobolev spaces. The analysis further demonstrates that the measure-valued weak solutions are stable under perturbations of initial data. The results generalize previous findings regarding the existence and stability results for measure-valued weak solutions in various settings.

This paper introduces a novel algorithm that leverages both TextRank and POSRank to identify appropriate search terms for software engineering refactoring tasks. Since standard search term suggestions often lack relevance for such tasks, we examine the potential of combining these two existing techniques. We have developed a new method that integrates TextRank and POSRank, which outperforms standalone TextRank in identifying suitable search terms. Furthermore, we apply positions and keywords from these algorithms to generate comprehensive search term recommendations for tasks involving code modifications. In addition to this, we have created a new dataset comprising 1,200 tasks and corresponding search terms extracted from the GitHub repository. We have also released the dataset and our source code publicly to facilitate future research.

Ultrasonically induced fluidization, a process where ultrasound prevents the sedimentation of particles in suspensions, has been extensively studied. However, the fluidization dynamics of such systems under ultrasound assistance remain poorly understood. This study presents a theoretical framework for describing the fluidization dynamics of rhea-acoustic gels, grounded in a dynamic model of ultrasound-absorption-driven micro-cavitation. The model demonstrates that the resulting fluidization dynamics are dictated by the balance of viscous, elastic, and acoustic forces. Consequently, ultrasound-assisted dynamics are directly linked to acoustic intensity, a relationship that can be derived from the steady-state shear modulus and the threshold intensity required for gel breakdown. Furthermore, the model predicts a fluidization dynamics characterized by a viscous regime, where the steady-state shear stress is proportional to the acoustic intensity, and an elastic regime, where it is proportional to the square root of that intensity. The study also identifies a distinct transition between these two regimes based on the ratio of elastic to viscous forces. The model's predictions regarding both fluidization dynamics and the viscous-to-elastic transition are validated against experimental data.

This manuscript presents a proof of the Collatz conjecture that relies on using mathematical induction to establish the base case, the inductive step, and a contradiction. The demonstration is built upon six lemmas, each proven to be true. The first five lemmas are used to set up the base case and inductive step of the proof by contradiction, while the sixth lemma serves as a tool to show that all integers greater than 1 eventually reach 3. Natural language processing (NLP) is a field where explainable artificial intelligence is particularly vital, as stakeholders require insight into the rationale behind machine learning decisions in tasks like document classification. This study introduces a novel framework for classifying documents with word-level interpretability, leveraging conditional value functions to pinpoint critical textual features influencing predictions. By applying this framework to various neural architectures, we generated an extensive dataset of local feature interpretations. Our analysis of this collected evidence demonstrates the feasibility of reverse-engineering an underlying decision rule from these local insights, effectively facilitating document classification.

Stable matching theory addresses pairing individuals in one-to-one relationships to ensure mutual satisfaction. This study examines an extension where agents possess public ratings, analyzing how rating-based preferences among agents and agents among ratings affect stability and utility. This setup reflects real-world scenarios such as online dating, job recruitment, and social networking. We propose a market equilibrium concept where agents' preferences regarding others are driven by these ratings, while ratings themselves are formed based on anticipated utilities from stable matching with specific agents. Our findings indicate that even slight deviations in agents' preferences concerning ratings can drastically alter resulting stability outcomes and utilities. Additionally, market equilibriums featuring coarse, binary ratings yield significantly lower utilities for participants compared to those allowing for graninal utility measurement.

This study introduces SummScore, an evaluation metric for English text summarization that leverages the power of large language models (LLMs). SummScore was developed to address the limitations of previous LLM-based metrics, which often struggle with summary diversity and establishing strong correlations with human ratings. To address these gaps, SummScore employs an input-conditional, multi-turn interaction pattern between an LLM "critic" and "questioner." This innovative approach yields a high correlation with human scores (Spearman's ρ=0.70) and successfully encourages greater diversity among model-generated summaries. Additionally, it exhibits low agreement with other automated metrics while maintaining high alignment with human judgment, indicating low bias. Empirical results confirm that SummScore outperforms current LLM-based approaches in both diversity promotion and correlation with human assessment.

We introduce a new approach for reconstructing compressible signals from their Fourier measurements, leveraging knowledge of how correlated the cross-data is. Our algorithm, named SPIDER, utilizes a specialized sparse recovery technique to enable signal reconstruction from a significantly smaller number of measurements compared to standard methods. Furthermore, we establish a theoretical result demonstrating that the recoverable signal sparsity increases with the cross-correlated nature of the cross-data. This finding is further supported by theoretical results and empirical tests showing that SPIDER outperforms existing algorithms in both handling a higher level of signal sparsity and requiring fewer measurements.

BeVFusion represents a pioneering end-to-end object detection framework designed for point clouds in Bird's-Eye-View (BEV) space, leveraging a unified representation for multi-view input data. It has demonstrated superior performance over existing benchmarks and exhibits significant robustness against real-world anomalies like LiDAR dropouts. This study introduces a novel approach, EnBEVFusion, which integrates external knowledge—specifically, a pre-trained convolutional neural network processing camera-derived feature maps—into the BEVFusion framework to create an enhanced, omnidirectional fusion model. EnBEVFusion unifies both multi-perspective LiDAR data and frontal camera imagery within BEVFusion to drive object detection. Our comprehensive evaluations across various scenarios confirm that this method surpasses current state-of-the-art results in speed, generalization, and detection accuracy.

This work examines how deterministic versus random initial conditions influence the statistical steady-state of fluctuating hydrodynamics equations. We demonstrate that the unsteady, stochastic Navier-Stokes equation yields a unique stationary distribution for dissipation and energy spectra, regardless of initial conditions, and that this distribution converges to the Navier-Stokes solution when fluctuations vanish. Consequently, fluctuating hydrodynamics provide a natural extension of deterministic fluid dynamics into the stochastic domain. Furthermore, natural and random initial data lead to identical statistical distributions, though they exhibit different transient behaviors.

We report a tabletop experiment demonstrating the spontaneous emergence of convection rolls and turbulence within air above a heat source, along with the replication of key features from galactoconvection and galactoconvection. When a laser passes through the resulting turbulent hot air, its diffraction pattern displays a stable central bright spot surrounded by disordered rings that fluctuate in intensity. Additionally, we developed a novel computational method capable of generating ring patterns that closely resemble laser data without requiring knowledge of the underlying refractive index distribution.

**Background:** Conventional design mining methods rely on identifying relevant projects from external repositories to inform predictions for new tasks. However, these methods often generate inconsistent conclusions due to the inclusion of irrelevant data, and their success is heavily contingent upon the user's ability to locate pertinent sources. **Objective:** This study aims to enhance conclusion stability, improve the identification of cross-project relevance, and reduce dependence on user-defined search strategies. **Method:** We introduce a novel model that leverages a differentiable search algorithm to directly optimize project selection based on the similarity between source and target tasks. **Results:** Empirical evaluation on design recommendation datasets demonstrates that this approach identifies highly pertinent analogous projects, delivers robust and stable inferences, and achieves state-of-the-art performance.

To support smart city initiatives, IoT devices are increasingly being deployed to gather and transmit data streams. However, the high volume and varying speeds of this data often overwhelm the capabilities of city data centers. H-STREAM is proposed as a solution that processes stream functions directly at the edge, enabling data analysis in real time. This approach leverages a blockchain protocol to securely manage distributed execution and ensure verifiable results. To enhance this architecture, we introduce a specialized consensus algorithm designed to balance computational loads among edge nodes, thereby reducing latency. Evaluation of the system demonstrates that it successfully surpasses current solutions by delivering lower end-to-end processing times and improved load distribution.

This study examines the impact of non-resonant diagrams on the vector-like $T$-partner ($T$-top) pair production cross-section, which occurs via effective contact interactions derived from a dimension-6 operator in the Standard Model effective field theory (SMEFT). We demonstrate that these background diagrams substantially affect the resonant cross-section and predicted production rates. Furthermore, we observe that the non-resonant cross-section exhibits strong sensitivity to the new physics scale, making the dimension-6 operator. Consequently, the prediction for the pair-production rate of the $Z$-top depends heavily on the specific parameter values chosen.

Copy networks have proven highly effective for abstractive text summarization, yet their application to generating SPARQL queries from natural language remains unexplored. This study introduces a new sequence-to-sequence Copy network architecture designed to automatically construct SPARQL queries without relying on pre-trained models. Our approach leverages the copy mechanism to directly insert relevant subgraph entities into the output, thereby reducing the need for extensive external training data. Furthermore, we implemented a novel loss function to address scenarios where standard copy network metrics fail to converge. Experimental results indicate that this proposed framework surpasses conventional sequence-to-sequence copy networks in generating SPARQL queries.

We introduce a new approach to examining the evolution of Computer Science disciplines by analyzing their publication venues. This method offers a distinct advantage over traditional co-authorship or keyword-based analyses, which often overlook the temporal context of development. We demonstrate that publishing venues provide a reliable proxy for field-level dynamics, effectively capturing the rise and maturity of emerging areas while reflecting the shifting interests within established fields. Additionally, tracking venue scope reveals the cross-overd boundaries between disciplines. We applied this methodology to evaluate the development of three specific areas: the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the field of Human-Computer Interaction, the transition of Artificial Intelligence from an academic pursuit to a core component of Computer Science, and the evolution of the field of Programming Languages from 1970 to 2020.

This study introduces a novel approach to verifying the robustness of closed-loop systems where both the plant and the controller are neural networks. Leverging recent methodologies from computer vision and machine learning, we formulate a robust control problem for these neural networks within a data-driven framework. This approach enables the integration of extensive simulation data to significantly lower computational costs. Additionally, we incorporate a data augmentation strategy to mitigate issues related to data dimensionality. The effectiveness of our proposed method is demonstrated through a simulation of a self-driving vehicle tasked with navigating around obstacles.

Clustering algorithms are frequently modeled using functorial approaches that map single objects to clusters within a category. This work introduces an extension of such frameworks, designed to assign cluster structures to single-linkage hierarchies—specifically addressing their current lack of general formalization. This new model resolves specific deficiencies in single-linkage clustering, notably the failure to handle non-invertible distance metrics and the absence of a universal clustering scheme. Furthermore, we demonstrate the utility of this extension by applying it to define and analyze the optimal single-linkage clustering scheme using category-theoretic tools.

We introduce a new class of low-rank tensor models specifically designed to handle video data featuring motion, an aspect often neglected by traditional streaming tensor completion (STA) algorithms. While most existing literature assumes data independence between adjacent slices, motion creates complex correlations across these frames. To address this, we develop the SR-SCA (Sparse SCA) algorithm, which exploits motion patterns to perform efficient and accurate tensor completion. The algorithm is computationally efficient, capable of completing a single frame of 1024×1024×3 in under 0.1 seconds on a standard laptop, and it is sparse in both the data and structural domains. Comprehensive experiments on moving video datasets demonstrate that our SR-SCA approach significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art STAs.

We establish that for classical Weyl groups, algebraic Nichols structures are invariably infinite-dimensional, with the sole potential exceptions being those associated with types $A_n$, $B_n$, and $C_n$. Subsequent analysis demonstrates that for any root system, the corresponding pointed, non-group-type Hopf algebra features a generic braided charge matrix that is invariably singular. This finding confirms conjectured results regarding the dimensionality of braided Lie algebras and indicates that, in general, these algebras are infinite-dimensional.

This study examines the statistical characteristics and scaling behavior of inertial waves in a rotating liquid drop, utilizing high-resolution, high-frequency data collected at various radii within the fluid. The analysis confirms a spectral exponent of $5/3$, consistent with the theoretical prediction by Gotoh et al. (2009), and demonstrates that the system satisfies the necessary conditions for inertial wave turbulence. Additionally, we identify and characterize coherent structures within the flow, which are associated with significant energy concentrations.

Graph normalization serves as a powerful approximation for optimization problems involving submodular functions, particularly for those defined on binary states. This study explores the relationship between the iterative graph normalization process for minimizing linear functions and the problem of finding a Maximum Weight Independent Set (MWIS) within a graph. We establish that the final state reached by this process corresponds to a valid 2-approximation for the MWIS problem. Furthermore, we demonstrate that any independent set achieving a weight greater than half the weight of the MWIS optimal solution is a valid solution. We also show that for bipartite graphs, this process converges to the MWIS problem's exact solution. These findings yield novel, efficient algorithms for approximating general submodular functions in bipartite graphs and provide a theoretical basis for analyzing the Graph Normalization method.

We investigate the electronic properties of a graphene monolayer subjected to $s$-wave superconductivity induced by a sinusoidal electric field and an orthogonal magnetic field. Employing the Bogoliubov–de Gennes framework, we identify two distinct types of oscillations within the Landau levels (LLs) triggered by these combined fields: standard Fermi surface oscillations and unconventional superconducting gap oscillations. Notably, the traditional Fermi surface oscillations vanish when the superconducting gap is present. Conversely, the novel oscillations in the energy gap are a unique feature of graphene, arising from the presence of zero-energy states at Landau level centers. These findings may have significant implications for graphene-based superconducting qubits, particularly those operating in the sweet spot.

This study presents new observations of the M dwarf binary CR Draconis at 1.6 GHz, revealing a radio source with a complex, multi-component structure. The data indicate a total flux density of 0.12 ± 0.01 Jy and a spectral index of 0.67 ± 0.05. Polarization measurements show a mean total of 1.2 ± 0.2% with a mean circular polarization of 0.1 ± 0.1%. The source's structure consists of a primary component aligned with the binary orbit and a secondary component positioned roughly 10° away from the primary in the direction of the companion star. Despite significant variability in the secondary component, the primary remains stable. The source's position angle aligns with the binary's orbital plane, and the presence of these two components suggests a colliding-wind interaction zone. Furthermore, the observed high collision velocity between stellar winds supports the hypothesis of a shock interaction occurring within that region. The total radio luminosity of CR Dra is estimated at 1.2 × 10^28 W, which is comparable to Jupiter's output. However, unlike Jupiter's highly polarized emissions, CR Dra exhibits low polarization levels. These findings suggest that the radio radiation from CR Dra is generated by shocks within the interaction region of the colliding winds.

Articulated Neural Rendering (AR) is a framework designed for neural rendering of dynamic objects undergoing articulated motion. While previous methods like Neural Fields and their extensions rely on fixed, pre-defined parameterizations for geometry and appearance, AR introduces a novel approach using neural fields parameterized by neural points. These neural points, which reside in a preliminary pre-defined 3D space, are transformed into actual 3D coordinates via a point-wise function derived from a latent representation of the object's configuration. This flexible parameterization capability allows for the accurate modeling of complex geometries and appearance variations across diverse configurations. A significant advantage of this method is its ability to handle self-intersections among different parts of the object, a challenge often encountered with prior techniques. The framework's efficacy is demonstrated through experiments rendering various moving objects, such as toys, animals, and food items, in motion.

While humans effortlessly recognize objects in images distorted by a factor of 10, artificial neural networks typically struggle with even minor deformations. This study proposes a solution to enhance deep networks' object recognition under severe distortion by integrating contextual information. We demonstrate that adding a global context module to convolutional networks enables state-of-the-art convolutional architectures to successfully handle heavily distorted inputs.

We demonstrate that specific Wilson loops in Chern-Simons theory correspond to the generators of the Askey-Wilson algebra. By employing the algebraic structure inherent in this algebra, we derive recursion relations and closed forms for these Wilson loops. Furthermore, we formulate conjectures regarding their correlators.

We introduce a trimer-based computational basis tailored for Quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) simulations of low-temperature lithium systems, significantly reducing the sign problem compared to traditional methods. Our approach constructs a basis set of single-trimer determinants by applying a single-determinants per trimer (DPT) framework to a multi-determinants per trimer (MDPT) formalism, which accounts for various spatial configurations of trimers within the simulation box. To validate this method, we applied it to a low-temperature body-centered cubic (bcc) lithium model. Our findings demonstrate that the sign problem is effectively mitigated, yielding a negative weight ratio of approximately 0.96 at 20 K, a result that aligns closely with recent path integral molecular dynamics (PIMD) data indicating zero-point motion is sufficient to melt lithium.

Language models demonstrate the ability to answer queries without specific task training during the fine-tuning process, a trait known as zero-shot learning. This paper investigates how model scale influences this capability by analyzing GPT-2 with varying parameter counts (ranging from 124 million to 1.5 billion) across three distinct datasets: a sentiment analysis task, a binary classification task, and a three-class task. We evaluate Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUC-ROC) scores using a standardized evaluation framework to ensure consistency. Results indicate a clear correlation between model scale and performance: larger models consistently outperform smaller counterparts across all tested datasets.

The determination of the nature of the electroweak phase transition is crucial for understanding dark matter and baryogenesis. A strong first-order transition is a specific requirement for a successful phase transition in the context of a matter-antimatter asymmetry. In the context of the Next-to-Minus Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (NMSSM), a strong first-order transition can be achieved by tuning the model's parameters. However, recent LHCb analyses have placed constraints on the parameter space of the NMSSM, which have implications for the region of the model that is consistent with a strong first-order transition. In this study, we investigate the impact of these constraints on the parameter space of the NMSSM and the region of the model that is consistent with a strong first-order transition. We find that these constraints significantly reduce the region of the model that is consistent with a strong first-order transition. We demonstrate that ALMA offers the capability to identify reliable redshifts at $z = 2 - 4$ with a precision of $\Delta z \approx 0.01$ in under 100 minutes, a significant improvement over current methods. This performance is achieved by utilizing the full spectral information captured by ALMA's high-resolution spectrograph, which captures multiple redshifted emission lines. We propose a new technique that leverages these data to obtain redshifts with greater accuracy and efficiency than traditional approaches relying on template matching. Our method's effectiveness is validated through tests on mock spectra and evaluations of survey feasibility.

We demonstrate that low-lying monopole excitations in U(1) gauge theories are directly linked to Dirac spin liquid phases characterized by a low monopole number. This finding is established by constructing a specific U(1) gauge model featuring a term that renders monopole excitations extremely rare. Subsequent analysis of the model's low-energy behavior reveals the presence of a spin liquid phase. Our results indicate that monopoles are essential to this phase, as evidenced by the spin liquid's energy scaling with monopole density. Furthermore, we observe that the spin liquid's properties remain invariant regardless of the gauge coupling strength. These insights offer a novel perspective on the nature of low energy excitations within spin systems.

We investigate the temporal explicit breaking of the $Z_3$ symmetry in one-dimensional Majorana quantum wires by analyzing both analytical and numerical results. Specifically, we examine a system composed of two interacting Majorana chains situated on a spacetime lattice, where each chain possesses a distinct hopping phase. While a single isolated chain exhibits an exact $Z_3$ symmetry, we demonstrate that incorporating a second interacting chain situated on a discrete time lattice explicitly breaks this symmetry. We analyze how varying the number of temporal lattice sites and temperature influences the symmetry breaking, observing that the breaking strength increases with a higher number of time slices. Furthermore, we observe a non-trivial interplay between temperature and this symmetry breaking.

This study employs first-principles calculations to examine the electronic and magnetic properties of the half-metallic ferromagnet Cr$_2$Al, which crystallizes in the AuCu$_2$-type structure. Results indicate that Cr$_2$Al exhibits 100% spin polarization with a saturation magnetization of 3.00 $\mu_B$/formula unit. The magnetic order is **ferromagnetic**, meaning all magnetic moments are aligned **parallel** to one another, in stark contrast to the **antiferromagnetic, layered order** found in Mn$_2$Au. Additionally, the material displays anisotropic electronic behavior, with a significantly higher in-plane exchange splitting compared to the out-of-plane component. These findings suggest a potentially higher anisotropy constant for Cr$_2$Al relative to CrPt and CrNi, thereby making it a viable candidate for applications in spintronic devices.

This study examines the thermal transpiration effect within canonical rarefied microflows, specifically gas flow through a horizontal capillary, utilizing the canonical ensemble framework. We employ the newly developed $\theta$-model, which accurately incorporates thermal transpiration, alongside the canonical probability distribution. By applying a perturbation approach to these elements, we derive analytical expressions for flow characteristics and compare them against results from direct molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. The theoretical predictions demonstrate excellent agreement with the MD data. Furthermore, this new method offers a computationally efficient alternative to direct MD simulation for modeling gas flow in microscale devices.

This study presents a new approach to few-shot semantic parsing that leverages large language models (LLMs) to generate extensive, high-quality task-specific synthetic data. Our method prioritizes the use of unannotated data sources, such as general domain knowledge, to create few-shot learning examples, while also incorporating external data from few-annotated sources, like programmatic synthesis databases, to enhance training data quality. We developed a specialized pipeline to ensure that generated synthetic data maintains consistency with the few-shot training distribution. Our approach demonstrates significant performance gains, achieving up to 10% accuracy improvement over state-of-the-art models in a zero-shot setting and up to 5% improvement in a few-shot setting. This method is versatile, applicable to few-shot learning problems across diverse semantic parsing tasks.

The upcoming high-luminosity run at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) demands significant enhancements in tracking detector performance to successfully track particles from heightened collision rates and preserve existing trigger and computing capabilities. To meet these demands, two advanced technologies have been developed: the Depleted Monolithic Active Pixel Sensor (DMAPS) and the ac-coupled Low Gain Avalanche Diode (ac-LGAD) sensor. Both are fabricated using complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) processes, enabling sensor readout via the same integrated circuit used for data acquisition. This approach offers superior mechanical compactness, reduced mass, and novel electronic functionalities. This study presents the latest progress on both technologies, focusing on sensor performance, noise levels, and the efficacy of ac-coupled readout circuits.

We report on the analysis of the low-mass X-ray AGN 2XMM J123103.2+110648, utilizing data from the Swift and NuSTAR observatories alongside archival XMM-Newton observations. This study reveals that the source exhibits variability in X-ray flux, spectral shape, and the fractional contributions of its components. Specifically, the spectrum is best modeled as a composite of a power law and a blackbody emission component. Notably, the relative intensity of the blackbody feature fluctuates significantly, while the AGN's spectral index remains relatively constant. Furthermore, the data indicate that the blackbody luminosity is anti-correlated with the power law flux. These findings are interpreted within the framework of the unified model for active galactic nuclei, which attributes the observed spectral and variability characteristics to the physical processes governing the system.

Magnetic B-type stars are known to possess magnetospheres, though their origin remains uncertain, potentially stemming from either the stellar interior or the accretion of interstellar matter. This study focuses on the B0.5 V star, $\eta$ Oph, to investigate its magnetosphere. We analyzed the emission lines of $\eta$ Oph using high-resolution spectra from the HST, VLT, and Keck observatories, alongside the data of a non-magnetic B0.5 V star, $\zeta$ Oph, as a reference. By comparing the two spectra, we identified spectral line variations attributable to the stellar magnetosphere. The findings suggest that the magnetosphere of $\eta$ Oph is not intrinsic to the star but rather formed by the accretion of interstellar matter.

We present a study of the star-forming galaxy Mrk 273, which exhibits a star formation rate (SFR) of approximately 0.1 M☉/yr derived from H30α data, alongside a significantly higher SFR of 0.3 M☉/yr inferred from total infrared (IR) flux. This discrepancy mirrors findings in other low-metallicity systems, suggesting that IR data alone may overestimate SFRs in metal-poor galaxies. To investigate this issue, we obtained new observations of Mrk 273 using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) at 850 μm. The resulting ALMA map reveals a compact, extended dust continuum source with a flux density of 1.0 ± 0.1 mJy. Comparing the observed 850 μm emission to the modeled spectral energy distribution (SED) of the galaxy indicates that the dust continuum is dominated by emission at longer wavelengths (>350 μm). Consequently, the total IR luminosity is estimated at LIR = 1.2 × 10^9 L☉, which aligns with the H30α-based SFR of 0.1 M☉/yr. This consistency demonstrates that the IR-derived SFR discrepancy in low-metallicity galaxies arises primarily from the contribution of older stellar populations to the infrared luminosity, rather than from dust properties.

This study examines stochastic elliptic partial differential equations with small noise coefficients, focusing on constructing approximate solutions via Gabor frames of the Nearest-Neighbor Kernel Method (NNKM). Established are rigorous convergence results demonstrating that NKNM's performance matches or exceeds that of the standard Galerkin method. Furthermore, numerical experiments illustrate the efficacy of these new theoretical findings.

This study introduces an innovative observer architecture tailored for nonlinear systems, specifically targeting deterministic epidemic models. By integrating a randomized clock with a feedback mechanism, the observer enhances state estimation accuracy. The design ensures that random measurement noise is randomized into a deterministic equivalent that is dominated by the system's drift dynamics. Leveraging the dissipative properties inherent in epidemic models, the scheme guarantees exponential convergence of the estimation error. The approach's utility is demonstrated through a case study on an epidemic model featuring a time-varying parameter, with results compared against standard observers. Additionally, the design methodology is extended to a broader class of nonlinear systems.

This study introduces a new approach to improve temporal knowledge graph embeddings by leveraging the time-series characteristics of valid time intervals. We propose a novel framework called Time-Series Attention Embedding (TSAE), which applies our specific type of temporal encoding to capture patterns across intervals. TSAE is designed to be lightweight, computationally efficient, and easy to integrate with existing models. Experimental results on three well-known benchmarks demonstrate that our method surpasses the state-of-the-art, achieving an improvement of 2.4% over the leading models. Additionally, we evaluated the method's performance on a real-world dataset, the 2018 Kaggle Uber dataset, and found that our approach outperforms existing models by 3.3%.

Kerr-lens mode-locking (KLPM) is the most prevalent technique for generating ultrashort pulses, yet its underlying physics remains incompletely understood. This study presents a theoretical framework that elucidates KLPM by integrating the concepts of self-focusing and power-dependent Kerr-gain. The resulting model is straightforward, capable of explaining the complex behavior observed in both planar and conical cavity configurations. Specifically, it accounts for the stability threshold of Kerr-lens mode-locking, a phenomenon previously unexplained by existing theories. The article further explores the spectrum of plane and conical cavities to characterize their distinct behaviors and similarities. Ultimately, this work offers a unified perspective on the diverse aspects of KLPM, paving the way for more advanced simulations and a deeper comprehension of the system's intricacies.

Federated learning (FL) is a distributed machine learning technique where a central server aggregates information from multiple local nodes to train a global model. In asynchronous FL, the server updates the global model whenever a local participant finishes training and sends their results, without waiting for inputs from others. This approach often results in frequent idle computing resources at local participants during waiting periods. We introduce a Partial-Sharing-based Communication (PSC) framework designed to mitigate these underutilized resources. By allowing participants to share only a subset of data samples with the server, the server can execute fewer concurrent asynchronous tasks, thereby reducing the waiting time for participants between batches. We further analyze the impact of this communication strategy on the FL global model's performance. Empirical results demonstrate that the PSC framework effectively enhances resource utilization and improves the efficiency of global model training.

This study examines the optical properties of a silicon-on-insulator (SOI) photonic crystal (PhC) waveguide, featuring a periodic array of holes within a silicon membrane that sits atop a SiO$_2$ buffer and a PhC-based back reflector. The periodic structure enables light to travel through the thin silicon layer, which is otherwise too slender for direct absorption measurement. By employing a Bragg PhC mirror as the back reflector, the effective optical path length increases, allowing absorption in films as thin as 1.5 $\mu$m to be detected. The experiment investigates the thin silicon membrane's ability to absorb specific infrared wavelengths critical for PhC waveguide integration, such as 1030 nm, 1550 nm, and 10 $\mu$m. Results indicate that the photonic crystal back reflector successfully enhances the detectability of absorption spectra in the semiconductor layer.

We introduce two novel functions capable of encapsulating the complex plane's exponential map dynamics, along with every complex polynomial raising map, within a compact domain. These functions also converge to a shared invariant measure for rational functions. In the context of real analytic functions, they satisfy specific differential equations and are expressible as the limit of an iterative process.

High-dimensional expanders are hypergraph analogues of traditional expanders, attracting significant interest due to their promising applications in complexity theory, coding theory, and cryptography. Although it is well-established that these structures yield robust expansion properties for random walks, their interaction with conductance remains a less explored area. This work introduces a novel conductance lower bound for high-dimensional expanders, effectively translating their topological expansion characteristics into separation between the top eigenvector of the Laplacian matrix and zero. Furthermore, we apply this metric to develop approximation algorithms for graph coloring and demonstrate that colorings generated by the basic Lasserre algorithm achieve optimal performance on random hypergraph expanders.

GdInO$_3$ crystallizes in the orthorhombic space group $Pbnm$, featuring Gd$^{3+}$ ions arranged in a bipyramidal coordination within a monoclinic-like simple hexagonal lattice. This structure supports two optical phonon modes, which are essential for analyzing the material's optical properties. Using the ab initio method, we calculated the phonon dispersion relations and optical mode profiles. Subsequently, these results were employed to generate a model for the infrared reflectivity spectrum, which aligns well with experimental data. Finally, various dielectric functions derived from different approaches were compared.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have become a dominant approach for learning on networks, yet their widespread application is hindered by the substantial computational costs associated with their non-sparse adjacency matrices. This paper introduces a new method for generating sparse adjacency matrices that retain the essential topological characteristics of the original graph, utilizing the Node Representation based on the Sum of Normalized H-order Adjacency Matrix (SNHAM). This technique leverages the inherent sparsity of the original graph to optimize GNN performance. We further propose a novel framework for node representation within sparse graphs, which incorporates node centrality metrics to derive an even sparser adjacency matrix that remains effective for various Graph Neural Network models. Experimental results across multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that these learned sparse matrices achieve performance comparable to the original dense matrices while significantly reducing computational expenses.

This study presents a novel design for the activation phase of effervescent tablets, utilizing a dual-chamber structure that maintains a higher local vapor concentration. Vapor from the activation zone is funneled into a secondary chamber, which not only improves vapor density but also lessens the impact of external airflow. To evaluate this concept, a computational fluid dynamics (CFD) model was developed and applied to simulate activation under two distinct scenarios: one featuring the proposed dual-chamber system and another representing a standard single-layer tablet. The dual-chamber approach demonstrated faster activation rates, a more uniform distribution of vapor, and superior performance in areas critical for gas-solute interaction.

We introduce a new nonlinear interference model that surpasses the GNR model in accuracy, specifically for observing the power-dependent behaviors of length-scale effects and polarization multiplexing formats. We demonstrate that this enhanced model is highly effective in explaining the intricate nonlinear interference characteristics of current and future optical networks.
